mainEntity.name: What should a meeting summary include?

acceptedAnswer.text: Include the purpose, decisions, action items with owners and dates, open questions and the next meeting. One edge case: Microsoft says people outside your organization cannot open a Teams intelligent recap, even with the recording link. For client meetings, paste the decisions and actions into the email instead of linking the recap.

mainEntity.name: How long should a meeting summary be?

acceptedAnswer.text: Keep it to 5 to 10 lines, which is roughly 50 to 125 words. Grammarly's guide gives that same 50 to 125 word range for most follow-up emails, and says longer ones can reduce the chance of a reply. If yours runs past 10 lines, move the discussion into the linked notes.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a meeting summary and minutes?

acceptedAnswer.text: A summary is a short, informal recap for action. Minutes are the formal record, usually approved at the next meeting. Under Robert's Rules of Order, minutes record what was done, not what was said, so even formal minutes skip the discussion. Keep minutes for board, HOA or other official meetings.

mainEntity.name: When should I send a meeting summary?

acceptedAnswer.text: Aim for within 1 hour, and treat 1 business day as the outer limit: Grammarly's follow-up guide recommends a meeting recap within one business day. For meetings that end late on a Friday, send a short version the same day rather than waiting until Monday.

mainEntity.name: How do I start a meeting summary email?

acceptedAnswer.text: Open with one line that names the meeting, then go straight to decisions and action items. Skip "Just following up" as an opener: Grammarly suggests stating the purpose of the email instead. If you are summarizing for someone who missed the meeting, start with the one decision that affects them.

mainEntity.name: Can I use the same template for every meeting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, for all 4 example types above (team, client, project and one-on-one), as long as the order stays the same. The exception is any meeting with legal or procedural requirements, such as a board vote or a contract decision.
